title: The Leaked Iran Deal Gives Tehran Almost Everything It Wanted. India's Oil Bill Depends on What Happens Next.
excerpt: A 14-point memorandum published by Iranian state media includes Hormuz reopening under Iranian control, $300 billion in reparations talks, and a 60-day nuclear deferral. Trump says the leak is fake. Oil has crashed to a two-month low.
body:
The full contours of a possible deal to end the Gulf war emerged on Friday, and they look nothing like what Washington has been promising.

A draft memorandum of understanding published by Iranian state media and corroborated by Western, Pakistani and Iranian sources speaking to Reuters outlines 14 terms that, on paper, hand Tehran nearly every demand it has made since fighting began in February. President Trump immediately denied the leaked version represents the actual agreement. Oil prices, indifferent to the dispute over wording, fell more than 3 per cent to their lowest level in two months.

For India — the world's third-largest oil importer, with 85 per cent of its crude coming from abroad — the gap between what was leaked and what was agreed is not an academic question. It is the difference between a fuel subsidy bill that keeps climbing and one that begins to shrink.

What the 14-Point Memo Says

The draft, published by Iran's Mehr and IRNA news agencies and confirmed in its broad strokes by multiple sources, includes terms that would have been unthinkable to Washington six months ago:

An immediate and permanent ceasefire on all fronts, including in Lebanon. The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz within 30 days, but "under arrangements made by Iran" — meaning Tehran retains operational control of the waterway. A complete lifting of the US naval blockade. Suspension of all sanctions on Iranian oil, petrochemicals and financial access. Discussion of reconstruction plans for Iran "worth at least $300 billion." Release of $24 billion in frozen Iranian funds during a 60-day negotiation window — with half disbursed before talks even begin. A reaffirmation of Iran's nuclear non-proliferation commitment, without any new curbs on its programme or existing stockpiles.

Conspicuously absent: any mention of Iran's 400 kilograms of highly enriched uranium, its missile programme, or its funding of regional proxy forces — all longstanding American demands.

Trump's Version vs. Tehran's Version

Trump took to Truth Social within hours: "The terms that Iran leaked out to the Fake News have NOTHING to do with the terms that were agreed to, in writing."

A senior US official, speaking anonymously, painted a starkly different picture of the deal: Iran's nuclear material "will be destroyed and removed," the nuclear programme dismantled, Hormuz opened unconditionally, and no money released until Iran performs. "This is a performance-based deal," the official said.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said the memorandum had "never been closer" but cautioned against speculation before it is finalised. A Western source told Reuters that if language can be agreed — the key sticking point is Israel's campaign against Hezbollah in Lebanon — the deal could be signed as soon as Sunday by Vice President JD Vance and Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammed Baqer Qalibaf, with Geneva as the likeliest venue.

Israel, despite jointly launching the war with the US, has been excluded from negotiations. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel would not be party to the memorandum.

What Markets Are Pricing In

The markets are not waiting for the text to be finalised. Brent crude fell over 3 per cent on Friday to $87.25 a barrel — its lowest since April 17. US West Texas Intermediate dropped to $84.57. Global equities rallied on the prospect of lower energy costs.

India's Sensex had already surged 1.2 per cent earlier in the day on early deal speculation. The rupee, battered to 95.35 against the dollar by months of oil-driven current account pressure, could see significant relief if Hormuz reopens to normal traffic.

But the caveats are large. The strait, which normally carries a fifth of global oil and LNG shipments, was effectively closed by Iran on Thursday when its military command announced that any vessel attempting passage would be "shot at." US forces said commercial ships continued to transit, but at severe risk. Even if a deal is signed Sunday, the physical reopening — demining, insurance reinstatement, convoy escort removal — could take weeks.

India's Stake

India's exposure to this negotiation is existential in the short term and structural in the medium term.

The oil import bill has already jumped 53 per cent between March and April. The government has extended ₹1.2 trillion to oil companies to keep fuel prices stable. The fertiliser ministry wants to double its subsidy budget. The fiscal deficit is drifting toward 4.8 per cent of GDP.

A Hormuz reopening would begin reversing these pressures, but not overnight. Oil traders at PVM Associates warned that global and regional crude inventories are historically low, meaning prices could stay elevated even after a deal. LNG contracts are priced on forward curves that won't adjust for weeks.

The Reserve Bank of India's latest projections assume Brent at $90 for the rest of the fiscal year. If a deal brings sustained prices below $85, the central bank's inflation forecast of 5.1 per cent becomes achievable and the case for rate cuts — currently priced out by swap markets — begins to rebuild.

For NRIs, the downstream effects are tangible: airfares between India and the US and Gulf have risen 15–25 per cent since February on fuel surcharges. Remittance purchasing power has eroded as the rupee weakened. Household budgets in India, funded partly by diaspora transfers, are absorbing food inflation driven by the same energy shock.

What to Watch This Weekend

The next 48 hours will clarify whether the deal is as close as both sides claim. If Vance and Qalibaf meet in Geneva on Sunday, a signed memorandum could trigger the 30-day Hormuz reopening clock and the 60-day nuclear negotiation window simultaneously. If the language on Lebanon — Iran's last major demand — cannot be resolved, the escalation cycle resumes.

India, with three dead sailors, a summoned ambassador, and a prime minister about to meet Trump at the G7, has never had more riding on a deal it has no seat at.
